clue.text: Digs weed in field near stable

parts.note: digs are lodgings, and a pad is slang for one's flat or lodgings
dock is a common broad-leaved weed

explanation.surface: Someone lodging in a weedy field beside the stables.
explanation.definitionFit: A paddock is a small enclosure where horses graze, usually beside the stables.

clue.text: Wrap up for this sort of holiday!

explanation.surface: An advert telling you to bundle yourself off on a cheap trip.
explanation.definitionFit: To wrap goods up is to parcel them; an all-inclusive holiday sold as one bundle has the same name.

clue.text: Do semi-skilled people teach it?

parts.note: household servants were thought semi-skilled workers, and the school subject of cookery and housekeeping sounds like the study of them

explanation.surface: A question about whether moderately trained workers give lessons in some subject.
explanation.walkthrough: Household servants are called domestics, so a joke treats the old school subject of cookery and housework as the science of servants.
explanation.definitionFit: The old school subject covering cooking, sewing and household management is what the clue describes.

clue.text: Roman to ring with six old pennies?

parts.note: a ring is round, so the letter O
VI is six in Roman numerals
d was the abbreviation for pennies in old British money (from Latin denarius)

explanation.surface: A Roman about to phone with sixpence in old money.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 British money was pounds, shillings and pence, with d standing for pence.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet of the Metamorphoses was a citizen of ancient Rome.

clue.text: Left side of street in Leek surprisingly, is "The Falcon

indicators.note: surprisingly says these letters turn up in an unexpected order
the left side of a written word is its first half, so the first three letters of the six are taken

explanation.surface: A pub sign in the town of Leek, on the left of the street, unexpectedly reads The Falcon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left side of' takes STR, the first half of STREET; 'surprisingly' shuffles STR with LEEK. Leek is a market town in Staffordshire. The stray quotation mark is in the printed clue.
explanation.definitionFit: This small bird of prey that hovers over roadsides is a kind of falcon.

clue.text: Sole highwayman?

parts.note: read the sole as the underside of a foot, the padding you walk on, and the robber as one who works on foot rather than horseback

explanation.surface: Asking whether there was a lone robber of coaches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sole' looks like 'only', but it is the bottom of the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for a robber who held up travellers on foot rather than on horseback.

clue.text: Wreckage floats freely at mouth of Mersey

indicators.note: freely says the letters move about without fixed order
a river's mouth is where it begins its meeting with the sea, so the first letter of the name

explanation.surface: Debris drifts loose where the River Mersey meets the sea at Liverpool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'freely' rearranges FLOATS into FLOTSA; 'at mouth of' gives M from Mersey, a river in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Floating debris from a sunken ship is the classic sense of this word.

clue.text: But square cuts can be made here!

definitions.text: But square cuts can be made here!

parts.words: But square cuts can be made here!
parts.note: a square cut is a cricket stroke and the square is the pitch area, made at a ground whose name means egg-shaped

explanation.surface: A paradox: right-angled slices from a rounded shape.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oval is a London cricket ground; a square cut is an attacking cricket stroke, so the shape that cannot be square becomes a venue for them.
explanation.definitionFit: Egg-shaped as a geometric figure, and also the name of the famous London cricket ground.

clue.text: His apparel merit change, working in a brotherhood of painters?

definitions.text: working in a brotherhood of painters?

indicators.note: change tells us to alter the order of the letters given

explanation.surface: A man's clothing earns him a makeover while he works among a group of artists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' rearranges HISAPPARELMERIT, all fifteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The style and principles of the Victorian Brotherhood of artists founded by Rossetti, Millais and Hunt.

clue.text: Conscientious office occupied, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the words are to be judged by their sound when spoken

parts.note: an office is a duty or post, and occupied means full

explanation.surface: A rumour that a diligent worker's office is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone conscientious is careful to do what is required of them.

clue.text: Appoint representative who will be on course

parts.note: to commission someone is to appoint them to a task
an agent acts as someone's representative

explanation.surface: Naming a deputy who will turn up at the racetrack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on course' means at the racecourse, where bookmakers take bets.
explanation.definitionFit: A bookmaker, who takes bets at racecourses, was formerly called by this name.

clue.text: Section of alluvial soil designated as well

indicators.note: Section of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A slice of riverbed silt marked for some purpose too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'designated' is a link word joining the hidden run to the definition 'as well'.
explanation.definitionFit: As well and too both add one more thing to what has been said.

clue.text: Got up as a wine

parts.note: rosé is a pink wine

explanation.surface: Someone stood, dressed up as a bottle of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got up' means 'stood' for the definition, but suggests 'dressed up' in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Got up and stood both describe rising from bed or a seat.

clue.text: Leather worn a little lower?

explanation.surface: A belt or boot made of hide sitting slightly lower on the body.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'lower' is a cow, an animal that lows (moos); a little one is a young cow.
explanation.definitionFit: Calfskin is fine leather, and a young cow is the little animal that moos.

clue.text: Runway for second journey?

parts.note: a trip is a journey

explanation.surface: An airfield's runway used for a return flight.
explanation.definitionFit: An airstrip is a runway, and the short form is common.

clue.text: Blackbird in stream

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
a rook is a black bird of the crow family

explanation.surface: A blackbird bathing in a stream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blackbird' looks like the songbird, but is split as black (B) plus bird (ROOK).
explanation.definitionFit: A small natural stream is a synonym.

clue.text: English concise dictionary? One left by order

parts.note: dict is the shortened, concise form of the word dictionary
a means one

explanation.surface: A reference book abbreviated, and a single copy left at the publisher's command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concise' looks like part of a book title, but tells you to shorten 'dictionary'.
explanation.definitionFit: This adjective describes something done by decree or proclamation, as an order from authority.

clue.text: Western law-officer is to assemble troops

explanation.surface: A sheriff's deputy in a cowboy film is gathering soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: In a cowboy film the federal lawman is a US officer of this rank, and the verb means to gather soldiers in order.

clue.text: Voice has faded about tea-time

indicators.note: about says one piece goes round the other

parts.note: passé means faded or out of fashion
tea-time is four o'clock, written in Roman numerals as IV

explanation.surface: A singer's voice has gone off around tea-time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Voice' is the grammatical term, as in active and passive. Tea-time in Britain is traditionally four in the afternoon.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar the construction where the subject receives the action is one of the voices of a verb.

clue.text: Skunk, standard spiteful creature

parts.note: a standard is a flag on a pole
a cat is a spiteful, malicious person

explanation.surface: A skunk described as a typically nasty animal.
explanation.definitionFit: In American use this weasel relative is another name for the skunk.

clue.text: Cheer up poor Neville, fifty short before noon!

indicators.note: before puts the first piece ahead of the next
poor says the letters are in bad shape and must be reworked
short says the name is lacking something

parts.note: the name is taken as written before a letter is dropped
L is fifty in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Friends trying to lift sad Neville's mood, fifty quid short before midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' removes one L (fifty) from NEVILLE, leaving NEVILE; 'poor' rearranges that into ENLIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: To cheer someone up is to make them livelier.

clue.text: Intimate view of finish at university

parts.note: close means finish or end
up means in residence at university, as in up at Oxford

explanation.surface: A close look at graduation day.
explanation.definitionFit: A photograph taken from very near shows a subject in intimate detail.

clue.text: Cheviot's first to get agitated being fleeced

indicators.note: first takes the first letter of the word it follows

parts.note: heated means agitated or angry

explanation.surface: A Cheviot sheep getting upset at being shorn.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cheviot is a breed of sheep from the Anglo-Scottish border hills, which suits 'fleeced'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be fleeced is slang for being swindled out of money.

clue.text: Strait-laced sort from up-train, changing

indicators.note: changing says the letters swap places

explanation.surface: A prim passenger getting off the train heading to London.
explanation.walkthrough: An up-train is a British train heading towards London.
explanation.definitionFit: A strait-laced person with strict morals is often called this, after the strict Protestant reformers.

clue.text: Boy eats one that is hatched

indicators.note: eats has one piece take another inside it

parts.note: a lad is a boy
I is one in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A boy eating an egg that has just hatched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hatched' looks like a chick breaking out, but means devised, as a plan is laid.
explanation.definitionFit: Plans laid are plans devised, just as a plot is hatched.

clue.text: A line-out is inappropriate…

indicators.note: out says the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: Commenting that a rugby line-out was against the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: A line-out is the rugby restart where players jump for the ball thrown in from touch.
explanation.definitionFit: Something alien to a setting is foreign to it, out of keeping.

clue.text: … match right and level

parts.note: a tie is a match, as in a cup tie

explanation.surface: A rugby fixture ending all square.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the surface to the previous clue; it plays no part in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A tier is one level of a stacked arrangement, as in a wedding cake or stadium.

clue.text: Canteen litter

explanation.surface: Rubbish in the dining hall.
explanation.definitionFit: A military dining hall has this name, and so does untidy clutter.

clue.text: Crazy officer retires with nothing

indicators.note: retires means the word draws back, so it is read from the end

parts.note: Col is short for colonel, an army officer
O is zero or nothing

explanation.surface: A mad colonel leaves the army with no pension.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish slang for mad, adopted into English for crazy.

clue.text: Green keeper?

parts.note: green means environmentally minded, and keeper someone who preserves, rather than a golf-course groundsman

explanation.surface: A groundsman who looks after a golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: The solver thinks of a greenkeeper on a golf course; 'Green' instead means caring for the environment.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who campaigns to protect nature and the environment.

clue.text: Traitor's first explanation of his crime

indicators.note: first picks the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: a reason is an explanation

explanation.surface: A turncoat offering his motive for betraying his country.
explanation.definitionFit: Betraying one's country is the offence a traitor commits.

clue.text: Usher for party, Roman-style

parts.note: a do is a party

indicators.note: style suggests a fashioning, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: An attendant at a Roman-themed party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'style' rearranges ROMAN into ORMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: An usher shows people in at the entrance, the role of a doorkeeper at a hotel or club.
